name: Swim front crawl properly
blurb: Most adults who "can swim" are fighting the water. Front crawl done properly is about body position and rotation, not arm strength — and it is the difference between 25 metres of thrashing and swimming a kilometre.
gear: Optional: a pull buoy and a kickboard
steps: Fix the body position first: press your chest down slightly so your hips and legs rise. Sinking legs are drag, and drag is what exhausts you.
Learn to breathe by rotating, not lifting: turn your whole body so one goggle stays in the water and your mouth clears in the bow wave.
Practise a six-beat kick from the hip, not the knee, with loose ankles.
Learn the catch: high elbow, forearm vertical, pulling water backwards rather than pushing it down.
Drill one thing at a time — single-arm, catch-up, side-kick — rather than swimming laps badly.
Build distance only once the technique holds; swimming tired reinforces the bad version.
tips: Breathing every three strokes forces you to breathe both sides and keeps your stroke even.
Lifting your head to breathe drops your legs and stops you dead. Rotate instead.
A few lessons with a coach will save you a year of self-taught habits.
proof: You swim 400 metres continuously, breathing bilaterally, and finish able to hold a conversation.
